1.x: In the first century, the Pharisees (strict legalists) and the Sadducees (wealthy aristocrats who controlled the Temple) were fierce rivals with major theological disagreements. Their unity here highlights the gravity of their opposition to Jesus; they set aside their differences to oppose him. They were not merely asking for a miracle; they were demanding spectacular, celestial authentication (like Moses bringing manna from heaven or Joshua making the sun stand still). They wanted a sign that came directly from God’s presence, rather than the healings and feedings they had already witnessed, which they dismissed as insufficient or potentially demonic.

4.x: “Adulterous” is a common biblical metaphor for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, akin to Israel’s idolatry depicted as marital betrayal (Hosea 2:2; Jer 3:8-9). The Pharisees prioritize human tradition, signs, and self-righteousness over God’s covenant, breaking their exclusive devotion to Him. Jesus refuses their demand for a “celestial sign.” Instead, he points to the “sign of Jonah” (a reference to his upcoming death and resurrection). Just as Jonah was in the belly of the great fish for three days and emerged, Jesus would be buried for three days and rise, which would be the definitive, final proof of his authority. “And he left them”: Jesus is not about satisfying the curiosity of those who are already hardened against him; he moves on to those who have ears to hear.

5.x: While Jesus is speaking about high-level theology, prophetic signs, and the corruption of religious leaders, the disciples are physically preoccupied with the fact that they forgot to pack lunch. They are still thinking on a purely material, literal level at this point.

6.x: Leaven (yeast) was a small agent that, when added to dough, would permeate the entire batch. It was commonly used as a metaphor for an influence, usually one that spreads corruption or permeates an entire group. Jesus is warning the disciples to be extremely careful. The “leaven” he refers to is the teaching, hypocrisy, and distorted legalism of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He is telling his disciples that if they let these wrong ideas into their minds, it will affect their entire character and ministry.

7.x: The disciples are still completely missing the point. When Jesus warns them against the “leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees,” they immediately think he is talking about physical bread. This reveals how preoccupied they are with their own lack of preparation. They are still interpreting Jesus through a lens of material scarcity.

8.x: Jesus calls them out for their “little faith.” He isn’t criticizing them for being hungry; he is criticizing them for failing to trust his provision and for being unable to see beyond the surface of his words. He is asking: “After all you have seen, why is your first thought still about physical resources?”

20.x: “tell no man”: In 1st-century Jewish thought, the term Messiah (or Christos in Greek, meaning “anointed one”) carried heavy nationalistic and military connotations. Most Jews expected a royal Davidic liberator who would overthrow the Roman occupation, re-establish Israel as a sovereign superpower, and judge the Gentiles. This idea came from a misinterpretation of various OT verses, such as Psalm 2:6-9, which pictures God’s anointed king ruling the nations and shattering opposition. Easy to read politically/militarily (see also 2 Sam 7:12-16; Jer 23:5-6; Isa 11:1-4,10-14; Daniel 7:13-14,27; Zech 9:9-10; 14:3; Psalm 110:1-6; etc). Hence, if the crowds caught wind that a popular miracle-worker was claiming to be the Messiah, it would likely spark an immediate, violent, nationalistic uprising. Jesus flatly rejected this model of kingship (as seen during his temptations in the wilderness and when the crowd later tries to force a crown on him in Jn 6:15). By banning the title for a time, Jesus avoids being framed as a zealot revolutionary or a political pretender to Caesar's throne. Also, men need to learn before they teach, and the disciples still had a lot more to learn.

24.x: Jesus lays down the radical, non-negotiable cost of discipleship. Fresh off rebuking Peter for trying to avoid the cross, Jesus turns to the entire group to explain that the cross is not just his destiny, it is the template for anyone who follows him. Jesus lays three distinct, progressive demands: Deny, Take Up, and Follow. (1) Deny: to “deny oneself” (aparneomai) goes far beyond giving up chocolate for Lent or practicing minor self-restraint. In the ancient world, this was the exact legal term used for disowning a family member or completely severing a relationship. To deny oneself means to utterly disown your own self-sovereignty. It means dethroning your own will, your own ambitions, and your right to self-determination, and handing total ownership of your life over to Christ. (2) Take Up His Cross: Today, people often say: “we all have our crosses to bear” when referring to a difficult boss, a chronic illness, or an annoying relative. But to a 1st-century listener under Roman occupation, the imagery of the cross was terrifyingly literal and specific. When a man took up a cross in the Roman Empire, he was not carrying a heavy burden; HE WAS WALKING TO HIS EXECUTION. A cross-bearer was a condemned criminal forced to carry their own crossbeam (patibulum) through the streets to the execution site. It signified total submission to the authority that condemned him, a public admission that his own life was completely forfeit. By telling his disciples to take up their cross, Jesus is saying: “Be prepared to die to your reputation, your comfort, and your very life for my sake.” It is a daily execution of the ego. (3) Follow me: To follow means to walk behind a leader, imitating their steps and absorbing their lifestyle. Crucially, Jesus does not tell them to go out and conquer; he tells them to follow. And where is he going? As he just revealed in v.21, he is going straight to Jerusalem to suffer and be killed. This verse is the direct antidote to the “human thinking” Peter displayed in v.22. Peter’s human mindset was focused towards SELF-PRESERVATION, and towards LEADING Christ (by trying to correct Jesus’ path), but Christ’s standard is about SELF-DENIAL and FOLLOWING Christ (submitting to his will, not our will). Peter wanted a Messiah who would conquer Rome and put the disciples on thrones. Jesus corrects him by stating that the path to true life is found only through death. If the King is going to a cross, his subjects cannot expect a path paved in gold.

25.x: The underlying Greek for the word “life” (psyche) has a dual meaning: it can mean your physical, earthly existence, or your eternal/soul true self. Jesus is playing these two meanings against each other. There are two paths: (1) Attempt To Save Your Life: If your primary objective in this world is to “save” your life (meaning to preserve your comfort, secure your earthly safety, hoard your wealth, and protect your ego from the offense of the cross), you will ultimately LOSE the only life that actually matters (your eternal soul). Self-preservation leads to eternal bankruptcy. (2) Willing To Lose Your Life: Conversely, if you willingly “lose” your life (surrendering your earthly ambitions, safety, and self-will, counting them as forfeit “for my sake”), you will find your true, resurrected, eternal life. Jesus is teaching that you cannot protect your earthly life and inherit eternal life at the same time. Holding on tightly to the world forces you to let go of Christ; letting go of the world allows you to take hold of Christ.

26.x: Even if you tip the scales with the entire physical universe (absolute wealth, total political power, supreme comfort and unmatched earthly prestige), it weighs absolutely nothing against the value of a single immortal soul. The world is temporary, passing away; the soul is eternal. To trade an eternal reality for a temporary luxury is a catastrophic business deal. “what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”: once a person dies and enters eternity apart from God, having squandered their life on self-preservation, what currency do they have left to buy their soul back? NOTHING. The wealth of the world cannot be spent in the courtroom of God. The Greek word for “in exchange” (antallagma) refers to a ransom price or a replacement item of equal value. The ransom price for a soul is completely out of human reach. After committing the mistake of falling into the self-preservation trap, Peter was now learning that avoiding the cross is the quickest way to absolute spiritual bankruptcy.

27.x: “the Son of man shall come in glory of his Father”: The “Son of man” refers to the man Jesus born of Mary, the visible manifestation, while the “Father” is the invisible deity inside that manifestation. Therefore, the Son coming in the glory of the Father is simply Jesus Christ returning in his full, uninhibited divine identity as both God and man: glorified Jesus. The Father is the divine Spirit indwelling the human body of the Son ("For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily,” Col 2:9), so this verse means that the human "Son of man" will return, but his human limitations will be completely obscured by the unveiled, radiant glory of the divine Spirit (the Father) dwelling within him. You will not see two or three persons arriving. You will see one visible person, Jesus Christ, exercising the absolute authority, judgement, and glory of the one true God (the Father). This is also what Stephen saw when he died. Acts 7:55-56 says that Stephen “saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.” Then Stephen prays: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” (Acts 7:59 KJV). Luke distinguishes between (1) the glory of God and (2) Jesus at the right hand of God. He DOES NOT distinguish between (1) God-the-Father and (2) God-the-Son; otherwise Stephen would’ve completely ignored God-the-Father since he only addressed Jesus. God is an invisible Spirit, He does not have a left or right hand. Being at the right hand means being at the position of privilege, authority, and power: “Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand OF POWER…” (Mt 26:64 KJV). That’s why you can speak of God being at the right hand of the poor (Ps 109:31) or the LORD at the right hand of David (Ps 16:8). And so Stephen’s vision presents Jesus as the exalted Messiah enthroned by the glory of the Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3). The man Jesus is seen in divine glory because he has been glorified by the Father. Jesus repeatedly says the Father glorified him (Jn 8:54; 17:1; Acts 3:13; 2 Peter 1:17-18; etc). The man Jesus is useless without the divine Spirit of the Father (Jn 5:30). So Stephen sees the same glorified Jesus that Isaiah saw on the one throne in Isaiah 6:1 (we know it’s Jesus because John says Isaiah saw Jesus in Jn 12:41). And we know the one on the throne is: (1) God (the divine Spirit) & (2) the lamb (the visible image of the divine Spirit), under one face and one name: Jesus (Rev 22:3-4).

“Reward every man according to his works”: On its surface, a phrase like “reward every man according to his works” can be easily misinterpreted as salvation by human merit. However, when we read the broader scope of the NT, it becomes clear that works are the evidence of salvation, not the engine of it. The key word is “reward” (apodōsei = repay, recompense, render back). This is not talking about salvation, since salvation is a gift, not the wages of works: “For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:8-9 KJV) & “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt… but believeth… his faith is counted for righteousness.” (Rom 4:4-5 KJV). If salvation were earned by works, it would be a debt God owes us. But Scripture says salvation is by grace through faith. However, believers are still judged (for reward, not for eternal life). We see this shown in 1 Cor 3:12-15: “Every man’s work shall be made manifest…” then Paul says: “If any man’s work abide… he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.” The distinction is important, THE PERSON IS SAVED, but the works are evaluated and reward can be gained or lost. So works affect reward, not whether the believer is saved (*** Catholics teach that “saved; yet so as by fire” refers to Purgatory; however, the context has absolutely nothing to do with purgatory. Fire is a common symbol used for judging, in this specific context, Paul talks about testing your works with fire to see whether they are gold, silver, or precious stones that survive the “fire”, OR the person’s works are wood, hay, and stubble, which would get “burned up”. What’s being tested are the works, not a person being “purified”; see v.12). Notice salvation is not lost here: "Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." (Mt 5:19 KJV). Also, the text says Christ judges ACCORDING TO (kata) works, not by means of or on the basis of work. A healthy apple tree is recognized and vindicated according to its apples. The apples do not make the tree alive; the life flowing through the tree produces the apples. At the final judgement, works serve as the indisputable, visible evidence of whether a person truly possessed saving faith and lived a life surrendered to Christ, or whether their faith was a dead, verbal profession. As the Reformers later summarized: “We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.”

28.x: This does not refer to the 2nd coming of Christ, as the immediate generation of listeners died centuries ago. The most direct explanation is found in the very next verse (Mt 17:1). In all three Synoptic gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke), this statement is immediately followed by the Transfiguration. Just six days later, Peter, James, and John are taken up a mountain. They witness Jesus irradiated in divine glory, flanked by Moses and Elijah. For these “some” (three specific disciples), they physically witnessed a visual preview of Christ “coming” in his royal, heavenly majesty before they tasted death. Another possible interpretation is that this “coming” refers to the end of the Old Covenant era. In 70AC, within the lifetime of many standing there, the Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. In the OT, God “coming” frequently refers to Him using foreign nations to execute historical judgement on a city or nation. For example: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at His presence..." (Isa 19:1 KJV) - this "coming" was implemented through a civil war and the conquest of Egypt by Assyria. Under this view, the destruction of the Temple was the visible manifestation of the Son of Man’s coming judgement on hardened Israel. A third potential view refers to the Inauguration (resurrection, ascension, and pentecost). This view looks at the cluster of events concluding Christ’s earthly ministry. Through the Resurrection and Ascension, Jesus is enthroned at the right hand (position of power & authority) of God. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit falls, and the kingdom breaks into the world via the ekklesia (the assembly of believers). Disciples like Peter and John lived to see this rapid, powerful expansion of the kingdom. Whether realized in miniature six days later at the Transfiguration, or historically in 70 AD with the judgment on the temple structure, the "coming" represents the visible, undeniable manifestation of the cosmic authority to judge and to rule of the Lord Jesus Christ.

2-3.x: Jesus does not offer a sign. Instead, he points out their inconsistency. He uses a common, practical observation of their day: the ability to forecast weather based on the color of the sunset. He is acknowledging their competence in reading earthly patterns, yet they are completely illiterate regarding the spiritual world. Jesus is telling them that they are standing right in front of the Messiah. His miracles, his compassion, and his teachings (which fulfilled the prophecies they claimed to study) were the “signs” staring them in the face. Their inability to see these things was not a lack of evidence, but a lack of will; they were choosing to remain blind because their hearts were hardened against him. They failed to detect tomorrow’s destruction in today’s unbelief.

9-10.x: Jesus uses their own experiences to challenge their doubt. He reminds them of the two miraculous feedings he performed. The logic is simple: If he has the power to multiply bread to feed thousands in a desert, he is certainly not worried about them forgetting to bring a loaf of bread for the journey. He is pointing them toward a higher reality: their relationship with him should transcend worries about earthly sustenance.
